how-to-quote-a-translation-project.html.text:
← Translator project quote calculator

How to quote a translation project, not just a word count

Treating every word the same undercharges a project full of new terminology and overcharges one a translation memory already mostly covers. A defensible quote weights the words, adds the work around the words, and checks the result against a floor you have already decided on.

Open the free quote calculator

What a flat per-word rate misses

Fuzzy matches are not free, but they are not full price either. A CAT tool reports a fuzzy-match percentage for a reason — treat it as the fraction of a full word's effort that match actually takes, and weight the word count accordingly rather than billing every word at the new-word rate.

QA, desktop publishing, and rush work are real hours. A quote built only from words-times-rate silently gives away review time, file handling, and any weekend or rush premium.

A minimum only binds sometimes. A flat floor exists for very small jobs. Once the calculated direct cost passes that floor, the floor is not the number to quote.

Worked example

1,800 new words, 1,200 fuzzy-match words weighted at 50%, translation productivity of 400 words an hour, a $45 hourly rate, 2 hours of QA, a $75 desktop-publishing charge, no rush fee, a $250 minimum, and a 25% target margin:

FigureValue
Weighted words2,400 (of 3,000 raw)
Translation time6.0 hours
Labor cost$270.00
QA + DTP + rush add-ons$165.00
Direct cost$435.00
Target-margin price (25%)$580.00
Quote floor used$435.00 (direct cost, not the $250 minimum)
Recommended quote$580.00 (the target-margin price, since it is higher than the $435 floor)

The $250 minimum never applies here because the project's real direct cost, $435, already exceeds it — the floor only changes the quote on jobs smaller than this one. The calculator's own headline number is the recommended quote, not the floor: it takes the larger of the floor and the target-margin price automatically, so a job like this one — big enough to clear its minimum, but still needing its target margin applied on top — never gets under-quoted by stopping at the floor alone.

Common questions

How do translators price fuzzy matches from a CAT tool?

Weight fuzzy words by the percentage of full effort they actually take, then translate the weighted total instead of the raw word count. 1,800 new words plus 1,200 fuzzy-match words at a 50% weight is 2,400 weighted words, not 3,000 — the difference is the effort a translation memory already did for you, and it should not be billed as new translation.

What should a translation quote include besides the per-word rate?

Direct cost is translation labor plus every add-on that takes real time: QA or review hours, desktop publishing or file handling, and any rush fee. Leaving these out of the quote does not make the work free — it just means they get absorbed into your hourly rate without you deciding to.

How do I set a minimum project price for translation work?

Compare a flat floor you choose against the direct cost the project actually works out to, and quote whichever is higher. A $250 minimum only matters when the calculated direct cost is below it — a project whose real cost is $435 should quote $435 or the target-margin price above it, not the $250 floor.

TRANSLATOR TOOLS / FREE

Quote the project, not just the word count.

A private translation quote calculator for freelancers. Weight fuzzy matches, add QA and DTP work, then compare the result with your minimum and target margin before accepting the job.

Project inputs

Why weighted words matter

New words, fuzzy matches, QA, and desktop publishing do not consume the same effort. This tool makes those assumptions visible so you can change them. It reports arithmetic, not a recommended rate or a promise that a project will be profitable. See the full quoting guide with a worked example, how this compares to a flat per-word rate, or to a CAT-tool platform like Smartcat.

Common questions

Why does a fuzzy match not count as half a word?

Because a fuzzy percentage is a discount on effort, not a rounding rule you apply after the fact. The calculator multiplies fuzzy words by the fuzzy rate before adding them to new words: at the default 1,800 new words and 1,200 fuzzy words at 50%, that is 1,800 + (1,200 × 0.5) = 2,400 weighted words, not the raw 3,000 — and it is that 2,400 figure the hourly-rate math actually bills against.

What's included in the quote besides translation time?

QA hours, desktop publishing, and a rush fee are added on top of translation labor, not folded into the per-word rate. At the defaults that is 2 QA hours × $45/hr = $90, plus a $75 DTP charge, for $165 of add-ons on top of the $270 translation labor — together the $435 direct cost the target price is built from.

What's the difference between direct cost and target price?

Direct cost is what the project actually costs you to deliver: labor plus add-ons, no margin. Target price divides that by (1 − your target margin), so at the default 25% margin the $435 direct cost becomes a $580 target price — the number that leaves 25% of the invoice as margin rather than 25% added on top of cost.

When does the minimum price actually take over?

Only when the direct cost of the work falls below it. At the defaults, direct cost is $435 against a $250 minimum, so the minimum changes nothing here; it exists to stop a very small job — a one-paragraph rush translation, say — from quoting below what it costs you to open the file at all.

Is my rate card or client's word count uploaded anywhere?

No. Every figure stays in your browser; there is no account, server, or analytics vendor involved in the calculation itself. Anonymous feature counts (which buttons were used) can be turned off entirely with the button in the footer.

Can I send the client a quote, not just a number?

Yes. Fill in your business details and the client’s, then “Print quote / Save as PDF” produces a one-page quote: what the project covers, the total in your own currency, the deposit split, how long the price stands, and a line to sign. Your hourly rate, direct cost, and target margin are not on it and are not printed — the client sees the price, not how you built it. Your business details are saved on this device so you type them once; the client’s details are never saved. The drafted scope is editable, and a line for work you priced at zero — no rush fee, no desktop publishing — does not appear at all.

Are my numbers saved, and can I share them?

Your last entry is saved in this browser's local storage, so refreshing the page or coming back later restores it — nothing is uploaded. “Copy shareable link” puts the same eleven inputs in the page's URL fragment (after the #) instead, so sending that link to a client or colleague opens this page with the exact same project quoted, without either of you retyping anything. A link takes priority over a saved draft when you open one.

vs-a-flat-per-word-rate.html.text:
← Translator Project Quote Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-word rate

A flat per-word rate is one number doing five jobs at once: discounting fuzzy matches, covering QA and DTP time, covering a rush premium, and leaving a margin. This page names no company or product — it compares against that generic pricing habit, using this calculator's own worked examples.

What each approach actually does

A flat per-word rate is fast to quote and easy for a client to compare: pick a number (often your hourly rate divided by how many words you translate an hour), multiply it by the word count, done. It treats every word — new or a 90% fuzzy match from the client's translation memory — the same, and it treats every project's QA time, file handling, and urgency as already baked into that one number, whether or not it actually is.

This calculator starts from new and fuzzy-match word counts weighted separately (a fuzzy match bills at its match percentage, not full price), then adds QA hours, a desktop-publishing charge, and a rush fee as their own line items on top of translation labor, then divides the total by one minus your target margin. Four numbers that a flat rate folds into one become four numbers you can see and defend to a client.

ProjectFlat per-word rate ($0.1125/word)This calculator
1,800 new + 1,200 fuzzy-match words at 50%, 2 QA hrs, $75 DTP, 25% target margin$337.50 — all 3,000 words at full price, no add-ons, no margin$580.00 recommended — 2,400 weighted words, $165 of add-ons, then margin
2,000 new words, no fuzzy matches, no add-ons, 25% target margin$225.00 — matches this calculator's own direct cost exactly here$300.00 recommended — the same $225, plus the margin a flat rate has no line for
Every project, regardless of mixOne number, set once, reused everywhereA number this project's own inputs produced, checked against your stated minimum

The two examples miss in different amounts but the same direction. The first project's flat rate ($337.50) is *higher* than this calculator's own labor cost alone ($270, from the 2,400 weighted words) — charging every fuzzy-match word at full price overcharges for the discount a CAT tool already reports — and still ends up $242.50 below the $580 this calculator recommends, because dropping $165 of QA and DTP and the entire 25% margin costs more than the fuzzy-match overcharge gives back. The second project has no fuzzy matches to miscount at all, so the flat rate lands exactly on direct cost ($225) and the whole $75 gap to the recommended $300 is the target margin, with nothing anywhere in a flat per-word habit to hold it.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Why not just quote a flat rate per word?

Because one flat rate is being asked to do five jobs at once: discount fuzzy matches, cover QA time, cover desktop publishing, cover a rush premium, and still leave a margin. A rate set from your own hourly productivity on new words covers none of those by default — it only covers the words themselves, at full price, with nothing held back for anything else the project needs.

Does a flat rate always undercharge?

On the two worked examples here, yes, but not for a single reason. Pricing every word at the full new-word rate overcharges for the fuzzy-match discount a CAT tool already reports — that part alone would push a flat quote up, not down. It undercharges anyway because it drops the add-ons and the margin entirely, and on both examples that gap is larger than the fuzzy-match overcharge, so the flat number lands below the honest one either way.

When does a flat per-word rate come closest to matching?

On a project with no fuzzy matches, no QA or DTP add-ons, and no rush fee, a flat rate set from hourly-rate divided by words-per-hour lands exactly on this calculator's direct cost — the gap that is left is purely the target margin, which a flat per-word habit has no place to put.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you type — word counts, rates, or the price you send — is sent to a server.

This page names no specific company or product — it compares against the generic habit of quoting a single flat rate per word, not a competing calculator or platform. vs-smartcat.html.text:
← Translator Project Quote Calculator

This calculator vs. Smartcat

Two different shapes: Smartcat is an account-based CAT tool, translation-memory, and marketplace platform built for running ongoing localization work. This page is a free, private calculator for one direct-client quote — weighted words, add-ons, and a printable quote, with nothing to sign up for.

What each tool is for

Smartcat is a cloud-based CAT (computer-assisted translation) tool and localization-management platform. Inside one account it combines a translation-memory-driven editor, terminology management, optional machine-translation pretranslation, project and vendor workflow, and a marketplace that connects businesses with freelance linguists and agencies. Word counts and fuzzy-match discounts are computed automatically against a translation memory the platform keeps between projects, which is most valuable when the same client sends recurring work and that memory compounds over time. It requires an account, and setting up a project means working inside Smartcat's own workspace. Smartcat's own pricing and plan terms are not repeated here, since this session cannot verify today's figures against Smartcat's current terms; only its well-documented scope as a CAT-tool and localization-management platform is described.

This calculator does none of what Smartcat's workspace does. It has no account, no translation memory, and no marketplace matching. It takes the new and fuzzy word counts, hourly rate, QA and desktop-publishing add-ons, a rush fee, and a minimum project price for one job you already have in front of you, and returns the weighted word count, direct cost, target-margin price, and the recommended quote — plus, once you have a number, a one-page printable quote for the client with the scope, total, deposit split, and a signature line. It runs free in any browser, needs no account and no project set up in advance, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I take recurring work from the same client and want a translation memory that compounds fuzzy-match savings across projects.Smartcat — that ongoing memory and workflow is what its account-based platform is built for.
I have one project's word counts and rates in front of me and want a defensible quote floor and target-margin price right now.This calculator — free, instant, private, no account or project setup.
I want to find new translation clients or work through a marketplace of agencies and businesses.Smartcat or a comparable marketplace — this page has no client-matching feature at all.
I need a one-page quote to hand this direct client, with the total, deposit split, and a place to sign.This calculator — the built-in printable quote is exactly that document.
I need CAT-editor features — a translation-memory workbench, terminology base, or machine-translation pretranslation — to do the actual translating.Smartcat or a comparable CAT tool — this page prices a project, it does not translate one.
Do I need an account, a configured workspace, or a shared translation memory to use the tool?This calculator: no. Smartcat's CAT editor and marketplace run inside a configured, ongoing account.

Most freelance translators get different value from each: Smartcat (or a comparable CAT platform) for the editor, memory, and marketplace behind ongoing or agency-routed work, and a private calculator like this one for pricing a single direct-client project honestly before a proposal goes out. This page's own figures are one project's arithmetic, not a translation memory, a marketplace listing, or a substitute for the CAT tool you actually translate in.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Smartcat?

They solve different problems. Smartcat is a cloud-based CAT tool and localization-management platform: translation memory, terminology, machine-translation integration, project workflow, and a marketplace connecting businesses with freelance linguists and agencies all run inside one account. It is built for ongoing or recurring localization programs, where a translation memory accumulates across many projects and a client or agency needs a system of record for the whole pipeline. This calculator does none of that. It has no account, no translation memory, and no marketplace. It takes the weighted word count, hourly rate, and add-on costs for one project you already have in front of you and turns them into a quote floor, a target-margin price, and a printable client-facing quote, instantly, with nothing uploaded and nothing to configure first. A translator already running recurring work through Smartcat's workflow gets that project's numbers from the platform it already operates in; a freelancer pricing a single direct-client job, or without a Smartcat account at all, is in the right place here.

Is this page affiliated with Smartcat?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Smartcat. Smartcat is named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not, based on Smartcat's own public site.
